unit.title: Introduction to Electrical Energy and DC Circuits

title: Kirchhoff’s laws — KVL, mesh currents and KCL
summary: Kirchhoff’s Voltage Law with a single-loop example; two-mesh KVL equations; Kirchhoff’s Current Law and two node-voltage examples.
transcription_policy: Notebook order and meaning are preserved; grammar and awkward English are lightly cleaned. Worked equations are kept source-faithful. Where the handwritten arithmetic conflicts with its own setup equations, the discrepancy is called out explicitly rather than silently corrected.

blocks.text: Kirchhoff’s Voltage Law states that the algebraic sum of all voltages around a closed loop is zero.
Equivalent class wording: in a closed loop, the sum of voltage sources equals the sum of voltage drops across the resistors.

blocks.text: The handwritten final numerical labels are inconsistent with the two boxed equations above. Solving equations (1) and (2) gives \(I_1=20/11\,\text{A}\approx1.82\,\text{A}\) and \(I_2=25/22\,\text{A}\approx1.14\,\text{A}\).
Kirchhoff’s Current Law states that the algebraic sum of currents meeting at a node or junction is zero.
Equivalently, the sum of currents entering a node is equal to the sum of currents leaving the node.

blocks.caption: Class-note redraw · KCL node-voltage example

blocks.text: Using the nodal equation exactly as written gives \(V\approx13.71\,\text{V}\) and \(I_{3.3\text{k}\Omega}\approx4.15\,\text{mA}\). The notebook values are the same to the intended one-decimal-milliamp approximation, but its intermediate arithmetic is rough.

blocks.alt: Notebook-style KCL practice circuit with a 15 V source and 1 kiloohm resistor feeding node V, with 3.3 kiloohm and 2.2 kiloohm branches from the node to the common return.
blocks.caption: Class-note redraw · KCL practice circuit

blocks.text: The handwritten working then simplifies this equation and ends with a value for \(V\).

Solving the starting equation exactly gives \(V\approx8.53\,\text{V}\). The notebook’s final \(90/11\) line comes from an approximate simplification and does not follow exactly from the preceding \(6.6\) equation.
